opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the basic reason is that bits are just so much easier to manipulate than atoms. In the digital world, everything is already in a form these models can read and write. Code, text, spreadsheets, web pages: it's all tokens, and the cost of trying something, seeing if it works, and throwing it away is basically zero. You can copy-paste, you can run a million experiments in parallel, you can undo. The whole loop of iteration is incredibly tight.

The physical world is a very different beast. You have to build hardware, you have to deal with supply chains, manufacturing, sensors, actuators, all of that. Things break, things are expensive, things are slow. Collecting data is hard because you can't just scrape the internet for robot trajectories the way you can for text. And then there's safety. If a model writes a bad line of code, you fix it. If a robot drops something or bumps into a person, that's a real problem. So the tolerance for error is much lower, and that slows everything down.

So my mental model is that you'll see a huge amount of change happen first in what I'd call the digital "information work" layer: software engineering, analysis, anything that happens on a screen. That's going to get rewritten pretty dramatically and fairly quickly. The physical world will come too, and I'm actually very excited about robotics and things like self-driving. But it's going to lag, because you're fighting physics and capital expenditure and regulation, not just compute.

Self-driving is a good example from my own experience. The demos looked amazing very early on, but closing that last gap to something you can actually deploy at scale took a really, really long time. I think a lot of physical-world AI will follow that pattern: impressive demos, then a long grind of making it reliable. Digital stuff can skip a lot of that grind, because the cost of mistakes is so much lower and you can iterate so much faster.

r001.rationale: The response says digital information is easy to manipulate and copy-paste, while physical work requires building hardware and dealing with slow, costly constraints. This clearly communicates why copying digital information is easier than moving physical matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that bits are a lot easier to move around than atoms. In the digital world, the cost of trying something is basically zero. You can spin up a model, run it a million times, iterate on it overnight, and the feedback loop is measured in minutes or hours. Everything is already in a form that computers can read and write, the data is there, the infrastructure is there, and the distribution is instant. You push a software update and it's on a billion devices the next morning.

The physical world just doesn't work like that. If you want a robot to do something useful in a kitchen or a warehouse, you have to build actual hardware, you have to deal with manufacturing, supply chains, safety, regulation, maintenance. Things break. The iteration loop is weeks or months, and every failure is expensive and sometimes dangerous. You also have way less data. The internet gave us this enormous pretraining set of text and images, essentially for free, but there's no equivalent dump of a trillion examples of robot arms picking things up. You have to go collect that, and collecting it is slow and costly.

So I think of it as a kind of tilted landscape. Knowledge work, writing, coding, analysis, anything where the input and output are symbols on a screen, that's where the models are already extremely capable and where I expect the change to compound fastest. The physical side will come, I'm actually quite optimistic about it, but it's bottlenecked by things that intelligence alone doesn't fix. You can't think your way through a factory ramp. And this gets at something I've said before, which is that I think a lot of predictions about AI are too aggressive on timelines in the physical domain and, if anything, maybe underestimate how much is going to change in the purely digital domain over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says bits are easier to move than atoms and describes instant software distribution to billions of devices, conveying that digital information spreads more easily than physical matter.

astra-6.text:
The digital world is just much easier to iterate in. If you have an AI that can do useful work on a computer, you can deploy it to millions of people almost immediately. The inputs and outputs are already digital, and you can run lots of experiments in parallel. There’s no factory you have to build.

In the physical world, intelligence is only part of the problem. You still need the robot, the actuators, the batteries, the supply chain. Things wear out. And when you make a mistake, you might break something—you can’t always just reset the environment and try again.

So I expect a lot of the early change to happen wherever the work is already mediated by a keyboard and mouse. Robotics can be enormous, but it has this additional deployment and iteration bottleneck. Software can move at software speed; physical things still have to be manufactured, shipped, and maintained.

r001.rationale: The response says digital AI can be deployed to millions almost immediately, while physical systems require manufacturing, shipping, and maintenance, conveying the ease of replicating digital work compared with moving physical matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the digital world is just a much easier environment for intelligence to act in. If you want to do something on a computer, the inputs and outputs are already digital. You can read information, write code, run it, and get feedback very quickly. And once something works, you can copy it and deploy it at enormous scale. You don’t have to manufacture a million robots.

In the physical world, intelligence is only one part of the problem. You also need hardware, power, maintenance, supply chains. Your robot has to deal with a huge variety of situations, and if it makes a mistake, something can actually break. So the feedback loops are slower, and deployment is much more expensive.

That’s why I expect a lot of change to happen inside computers first. It’s not that the physical world won’t change. It’s that software can move at software speeds, while robotics still has to move through the constraints of the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says working software can be copied and deployed at enormous scale, while physical deployment requires manufacturing robots, identifying the ease of copying digital work compared with moving or producing physical matter.
